o: The left adrenal has the splenic vessels and pancreatic body in front, the aorta medially and the psoas behind
The adrenals lie within Gerota fascia, next to the crus of the diaphragm
The right gland is crescentic and the left triangular
A torn right adrenal vein (short, entering the IVC posterolaterally) is repaired by rotating the IVC
e: Right triangular, left crescentic. The right adrenal lies higher than the left, even though the right kidney lies lower. The tail of the pancreas can lie against the left upper pole and adrenal, so it is easily injured.

q: A young man with congenital adrenal hyperplasia has bilateral testicular masses. Best interpretation:
o: Lymphoma
Leydig cell tumours
Testicular adrenal rests, which lie along the path of gonadal descent and can grow large in CAH; avoid unnecessary orchidectomy
Bilateral germ cell tumours: orchidectomy
e: Rests also occur near the coeliac axis. At birth the adrenal has fetal and adult zones and weighs about twice the adult gland. It shrinks after birth and keeps maturing until about age 3, with the zona reticularis last. CAH patients also have a high risk of benign adrenal adenomas.

q: Which statement about adrenal hormone physiology is FALSE?
o: Cortisol is circadian, peaking in the early morning with a low point near 11 pm
With continued aldosterone excess, the kidney 'escapes' sodium retention, so oedema is unusual
Salt loading suppresses aldosterone equally in normal people and in patients with aldosteronoma
Renin rises with low renal perfusion pressure, renal sympathetic activity and low sodium
e: Salt loading suppresses aldosterone and renin in normal people but not with autonomous secretion. This is the basis of confirmatory testing.

q: After bilateral adrenalectomy for refractory Cushing disease, which complication occurs in up to 30%?
o: Pituitary apoplexy in all
Conn syndrome
Hyperthyroidism
Nelson syndrome: an enlarging pituitary adenoma with raised intracranial pressure and pressure on the optic chiasm
e: Transsphenoidal surgery cures 60–80%, with about 25% relapsing. Bilateral adrenalectomy needs a careful multidisciplinary decision.

q: Which is NOT a feature of adrenal crisis?
o: Hypotension not responding to fluids
Priapism
Hypoglycaemic seizures in children, with hyperkalaemia
Abdominal pain mimicking an acute abdomen, with nausea and fever
e: Commonest cause: autoimmune adrenalitis in the US, tuberculosis in developing countries. After removing a cortisol-secreting tumour, crisis is likely because the other adrenal is suppressed.

o: Chromogranin A has been used to confirm phaeochromocytoma, and the review names PET as its preferred phaeochromocytoma imaging
Myelolipoma (fat with blood-forming tissue) is benign and needs no further treatment once removed
Adrenal metastases are rare
The four types of adrenal cyst are pseudocyst, endothelial, epithelial and parasitic, and about 7% are associated with malignancy
e: Adrenal metastases are common, most often from lung, breast, kidney and melanoma.

q: When should the ipsilateral adrenal be removed at radical nephrectomy?
o: Never
Only in left-sided tumours
Always (Robson)
Only with a large (T2) upper-pole tumour, an abnormal adrenal on imaging, or tumour thrombus reaching the adrenal vein level
e: Robson's 1950s operation included routine adrenalectomy. That is no longer standard.

q: During a right adrenalectomy for a large mass, which event causes renal infarction rather than bleeding?
o: Ligation of an upper-pole renal artery branch
Avulsion of a hepatic vein branch
Breaching the adrenal capsule
Avulsion of the adrenal vein from the IVC
e: The right medulla receives preganglionic sympathetic fibres. The right gland sits above the medial upper pole, close to the diaphragm behind.

o: Incise the diaphragm circumferentially to avoid phrenic nerve injury; the left adrenal can be reached through the gastrocolic or lienorenal ligament, the transverse mesocolon or the lesser sac
An inadvertent SMV ligation can be observed
Incise the diaphragm radially in a thoracoabdominal approach
Pancreatic leak is managed by immediate reoperation
e: A drain fluid high in amylase and triglyceride suggests a pancreatic leak, treated with bowel rest and TPN. SMV ligation needs revascularisation and bowel resection.

q: Which statement about the bony pelvis and ligaments is FALSE?
o: The female pelvic inlet is oval and wider, while the male inlet is heart-shaped
The ureter lies lateral to the front part of the uterosacral ligament, which inserts on the cervix and upper vagina
The round ligament ends in the uterus and is the male equivalent of the spermatic cord
The pelvic inlet faces forwards, directing abdominal pressure onto bone
e: The round ligament leaves through the internal ring, crosses the external iliac artery and ends in the labia majora. Its male equivalent is the gubernaculum.

o: The clitoral cavernous nerves come from the inferior hypogastric plexus
The peritoneum can be entered through the posterior vaginal fornix
Sacrospinous fixation puts the sacral plexus and pudendal nerve, just behind the ligament, at risk
The lower vagina drains to the para-aortic nodes
e: Lower vagina (internal pudendal artery): drains to sacral, common iliac and superficial inguinal nodes. Upper vagina (uterine arteries): drains to the iliac nodes.

o: The transversalis fascia belongs to the outer layer and is continuous with the endopelvic fascia
Translabial ultrasound compresses the tissue and cannot show mesh or bulking agents
The perineal body is where the bulbospongiosus, external anal sphincter and transverse perineal muscles meet
An episiotomy is angled laterally to protect the external anal sphincter
e: Translabial ultrasound does not distort the tissue and shows mesh, bulking agents and urethral implants. MRI is the most complete radiation-free imaging of the female pelvis.

o: A direct inguinal hernia lies medial to the inferior epigastric vessels; the conjoint tendon (internal oblique plus transversalis) strengthens the back wall
The superficial inferior epigastric vessels in Camper fascia bleed at groin incisions and port sites
The sacrotuberous ligament separates the greater and lesser sciatic foramina
The superior vesical artery arises from the obliterated umbilical artery
e: The sacrospinous ligament separates them. The pelvic plexus receives the superior hypogastric nerves, the pelvic sympathetic trunks and parasympathetic fibres from S2–4.

o: The trigone has superficial (ureteric), deep (from Waldeyer sheath) and detrusor layers; the Mercier bar runs between the orifices and Bell muscle from the orifices to the bladder neck
The ureter crosses in front of the common iliac artery
The cavernous nerves pass the seminal vesicle tips and lie closest to the prostate at the apex
The infant bladder is a pelvic organ
e: The infant bladder lies in the abdomen and may reach above the umbilicus. The prostate drains mainly to the obturator and internal iliac nodes, and sometimes directly to the presacral and external iliac nodes. Denonvilliers fascia separates the prostate from the rectum.

q: Which surgical anatomy statement is correct?
o: The male bladder neck has little sympathetic innervation
Retrograde urethrography shows tumour invasion depth

Ligate the pedicles close to the bladder to spare the pelvic plexus; the lateral pedicle lies lateral to the ureter and the posterior pedicle posteromedial; MRI (T1 with gadolinium and T2) stages urethral tumours best
Ligate the cystectomy pedicles at the internal iliac origin to preserve potency
e: The male bladder neck has rich sympathetic innervation and a complete smooth-muscle ring. In Fournier gangrene the spermatic fasciae are usually spared, but in practice debridement goes down to the tunica vaginalis.

o: ATP is the main transmitter for normal human bladder contraction
Acetylcholine and ATP provide most excitatory input to the detrusor, with NO and VIP also released
ATP acts on P2X and P2Y receptors and contributes to overactivity and pain
A nerve action potential is caused by sodium influx, and keeping the resting potential needs energy
e: In healthy humans contraction is mainly cholinergic, and ATP becomes more important in disease. Sympathetic preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine. β3 receptors are present both peripherally and centrally.

o: The urothelium is a passive barrier with no signalling role
During filling, the sympathetic reflex inhibits the detrusor and closes the outlet (negative feedback)
The guarding reflex: bladder afferent input activates pudendal motor neurons, increasing external sphincter activity
Central serotonergic activity suppresses voiding
e: The urothelium releases NO, ATP, acetylcholine, substance P and prostaglandins, and umbrella cells change shape as the bladder fills. Normal compliance comes from passive viscoelastic properties plus active neural signals. Distension reduces bladder wall blood flow, especially in a poorly compliant bladder.

o: Reflex voiding occurs only in normal adults

Switching from storage to voiding can be reflex (infants, spinal cord injury) or voluntary; voiding starts with sphincter relaxation; Barrington described a facilitatory urethra-to-bladder reflex; Nathan described filling sensations
Urethral relaxation in voiding is caused by acetylcholine
Voiding starts with sphincter contraction
e: NO from parasympathetic nerves relaxes urethral smooth muscle. The limbic system (safety) and prefrontal cortex (social appropriateness) decide when the PAG–PMC switch is allowed to operate.

o: Obstruction causes collagen changes, enlargement of sensory and motor neurons, and denervation supersensitivity
After spinal cord injury, a C-fibre-driven spinal reflex (involving NGF) develops; many C-fibres are normally silent and are recruited in disease
Bowel–bladder cross-sensitisation may underlie chronic pelvic pain; interstitial cystitis urine has antiproliferative factor (APF) and more ATP; the water-avoidance stress model mimics it best
A low voiding Pdet in women always means detrusor underactivity
e: Women can void at low pressure because urethral resistance is low. Ageing reduces bladder sensation, contractility and urethral pressure. Mice lacking BK channels or β1-integrin develop overactivity. Connexin-43 gap junctions follow a daily rhythm. Myofibroblasts and interstitial cells link the urothelium and nerves.

o: Causes of SUI include loss of urethral support, loss of the urothelial seal and reduced spinal serotonin
Isolated nocturia comes from nocturnal polyuria, sleep apnoea and leg oedema; antimuscarinics in urgency act through the 'motor-sensory' mechanism
Female continence relies on the hammock, submucosal blood vessels, the guarding reflex and sympathetic tone
Smooth and striated muscle differ only because cross-bridge cycling happens in smooth muscle alone
e: Both use cross-bridge cycling. Striated muscle has visible striations and no intermediate filaments. Smooth muscle works over a far wider range of lengths. The female external sphincter is horseshoe-shaped over the front of the urethra. Levator ani does not encircle the front of the urethra.

o: Seminal vesicles are commonly affected by primary disease
Prostate epithelium contains basal, intermediate and neuroendocrine cells; stroma contains smooth muscle, fibroblasts and connective tissue
Sex accessory tissues are the prostate, seminal vesicles, ampullae and bulbourethral glands (not the tunica albuginea)
Testosterone should be measured in the morning because of daily variation
e: Seminal vesicles are very resistant to disease. The prostate has a rich autonomic nerve plexus.

q: Which statement about the androgen receptor is FALSE?
o: It never returns to the cytoplasm once in the nucleus
Mice lacking oestrogen receptor α or β still have normal prostates, so oestrogens are not needed for prostate development
It dimerises head-to-head on androgen response elements whether they are direct or inverted repeats
After binding ligand it leaves its chaperones, dimerises and enters the nucleus via its nuclear localisation signal (Ran-dependent, ATP-dependent)
e: It shuttles back to the cytoplasm. The nuclear matrix is its main binding target in the nucleus. Acid phosphatase from the prostate can be raised in cancer, and also in Paget disease, osteoporosis and bone metastases.

o: Prevalence is the number of existing cases at a given date, while incidence is new cases per year
The placebo response depends on baseline severity (regression to the mean plus the doctor–patient effect)
Flow rate falls with age only in men
Reported rates of acute retention range from under 5 to over 130 per 1000 man-years, depending on the population
e: Flow falls with age in both sexes, and bladder fibrosis occurs in both. Trabeculation is due to more detrusor collagen. Serum oestrogen rises with age, and the prostate has oestrogen receptors. Much male LUTS comes from age-related detrusor dysfunction, not the prostate.

o: In the first terazosin trial, symptom scores fell by about 22%
Treating LUTS reliably abolishes detrusor overactivity
Dizziness is common with terazosin and doxazosin because they also block α1B receptors
Uroselective α-blockers act mainly on α1A and α1D receptors
e: Detrusor overactivity may persist after treatment. β1 receptors are not a drug target in LUTS. Recurrent retention is an indication for surgery. α-blockers improve the chance of a successful trial without catheter, and 5-ARIs reduce the risk of retention.

q: Six weeks after TURP for long-standing obstruction with detrusor overactivity, a man still has urgency and frequency, with sterile urine. Best step:
o: Urodynamics now
Check post-void residual, reassure and monitor; give an antimuscarinic or β3 agonist if emptying is adequate
Immediate cystoscopy for residual tissue
Restart 5-ARI and antibiotics
e: Storage symptoms often persist or worsen for months after relieving long-standing obstruction, so warn patients beforehand.

q: Which statement about TUR syndrome is FALSE?
o: Excess glycine can release ammonia and cause encephalopathy
Transient blindness indicates central nervous system toxicity
It occurs commonly with HoLEP and bipolar TURP
Absorbing non-sodium irrigant causes dilutional hyponatraemia, with confusion, nausea, visual disturbance, hypertension and bradycardia
e: Saline-based techniques (bipolar TURP, HoLEP, laser vaporisation) essentially remove the risk. Sham-controlled trials (microwave thermotherapy, prostatic urethral lift) showed significant falls in symptom score and even better flow, and sham procedures were well tolerated.

o: HoLEP gives results comparable to open prostatectomy but has a steep learning curve, and serious injuries mostly come from the morcellator
PVP is very safe, with encouraging results in anticoagulated patients
PUL and water vapour therapy preserve erection and ejaculation better, but long-term durability is uncertain
Perioperative antibiotics are no longer needed for TURP
e: Do not neglect antibiotic cover, because serious infections still happen. Patients should usually try medical treatment first. Choose a technique using both patient and surgeon factors.

o: Robotic simple prostatectomy needs more transfusions and a longer stay than open surgery
Both suprapubic and retropubic operations are done in the space of Retzius
Compared with TURP it removes the adenoma completely under direct vision, with lower retreatment and no TUR syndrome
The dorsal vein complex need not be controlled before enucleation in a suprapubic prostatectomy
e: Robotic surgery means less bleeding, fewer transfusions, less bladder irrigation and a shorter stay. Simple prostatectomy suits men who cannot lie in lithotomy. Suprapubic is preferred in obesity. Risks include incontinence, ED, retrograde ejaculation, UTI, bladder neck contracture, stricture and transfusion. Cystoscopy helps estimate size and is needed with haematuria, stricture, stones or diverticulum.

o: Mortality has fallen since 1991 and, in white men, is now below pre-PSA levels
Incidence and mortality are lowest in African American and Jamaican men
In the US, prostate cancer is the commonest visceral cancer in men and the third leading cause of cancer death
PSA testing has shifted diagnosis to younger age and earlier clinical and pathological stage
e: They are highest in African American and Jamaican men. In the ERSPC screening trial, deaths fell by 20–27% early on and up to 44% with longer follow-up.

o: Primary prostate cancer has two molecular subtypes
Chronic inflammation and proliferative inflammatory atrophy (PIA) may contribute; vitamin D modulates risk; smoking increases recurrence and death
GWAS have found more than 100 risk SNPs; multi-SNP panels separate very low from very high risk but do not predict aggressiveness
HOXB13 and BRCA greatly increase risk, and BRCA tumours are more aggressive
e: There are seven subtypes: four defined by gene fusions (ERG, ETV1, ETV4, FLI1) and three by mutations (SPOP, FOXA1, IDH1). Methylation patterns also separate them. Stem cells are the origin of clonal expansion. Effective chemoprevention needs non-toxic agents that block specific steps in carcinogenesis.

o: PSA is a kallikrein; ectopic expression occurs in breast, adrenal and renal carcinomas
Circulating tumour cells and ctDNA have no role in advanced disease
About 70% of serum PSA is bound to α2-macroglobulin, α1-protease inhibitor and α1-antichymotrypsin
Ejaculation can falsely raise PSA
e: They are promising biomarkers in advanced disease. The book says PSMA is also found in the central nervous system and intestine, and it is now a key imaging target.

q: Which statement about TRUS is FALSE?
o: The prostate has five divisions: anterior fibromuscular stroma, transition, central, periurethral and peripheral zones
The normal adult prostate is 20–25 g, stable until about age 50; the biopsy needle path is best seen in the sagittal plane
Hypoechoic lesions are cancer in about 80%
Volume uses three measurements in an ellipse formula; planimetry is used when more accuracy is needed
e: Hypoechoic lesions are cancer in only about 20%. Seeds from an ideal permanent implant are spread evenly with sparing around the urethra. Newer targeted methods include Doppler, elastography, MRI with DWI and DCE, spectroscopy and fusion biopsy.

o: Transperineal biopsy samples the apex better and may cause fewer infections; men without a rectum can have transperineal or CT-guided biopsy
After several negative biopsies, cancer is most likely in the anterior zone and apex (template or fusion biopsy)
Isolated transition-zone tumours occur in under 5%
Endocarditis-risk patients get oral ciprofloxacin only
e: The book's regimen for endocarditis risk or prostheses was IV ampicillin (vancomycin if allergic) plus gentamicin, then a fluoroquinolone. Most advise a self-given enema beforehand. Complications include febrile UTI, bacteraemia, prostatitis, bleeding, haematospermia, retention and sepsis.

o: Low-grade PIN does not increase cancer risk
The prostate lacks a discrete histological capsule
Favourable biopsy findings reliably predict a favourable prostatectomy specimen
Hormone therapy causes atrophy and squamous metaplasia and can make cancers look falsely higher grade
e: Adverse biopsy findings predict adverse surgical findings, but favourable ones do not guarantee favourable findings. Primary urothelial carcinoma of the prostate invades the bladder neck: over 50% are T3/T4 and 20% have distant metastases at presentation.

o: PSA under 1 ng/mL at age 40–45 may justify less frequent testing
DRE causes a large, clinically important rise in PSA
A tertiary Gleason pattern is reported when a small focus of higher grade is present
PSA is lower in hypogonadal men and on statins; BPH surgery lowers PSA
e: DRE does not cause a meaningful PSA change, while ejaculation can for up to 24 hours. African American men have higher PSA levels. MRI with DWI and DCE improves specificity.

o: Shared decision-making reduces decision regret, but the urologist's recommendation still has the most influence
Previous TURP increases early urinary toxicity after radiotherapy; waiting 6–8 weeks reduces incontinence and stricture
CAPRA predicts only competing mortality
The UCSF-CAPRA score (age, PSA, stage, Gleason, % positive cores) separated 5-year recurrence-free survival from 85% to 8%
e: CAPRA also predicts cancer-specific mortality whatever the treatment. Radical prostatectomy is the oldest treatment and still the gold standard. A rising PSA is the earliest sign of recurrence, but not every man with biochemical recurrence develops metastases.

o: Brachytherapy is the preferred treatment for high-volume, high-risk disease
The commonest late complications of radical prostatectomy are ED, incontinence, hernia and stricture
Erectile recovery depends on age, potency before surgery, extent of nerve sparing and surgical era; continence recovery depends on age
Urinary symptoms are more common after brachytherapy than EBRT, especially with BPH
e: Brachytherapy alone is rarely used for high-volume, high-risk disease. Adjuvant radiotherapy reduces relapse in high-risk features but did not improve overall survival in the chapter's analysis. Salvage radiotherapy works best with a late, slowly rising PSA, low grade, and no seminal vesicle or nodal disease.

o: The negative predictive value of MRI is the same whatever the underlying risk
Microfocal cancer is found in 50–60% of middle-aged men
Misattributed grade (25–30%) is much commoner than true progression (1–2.3% a year)
Use surveillance visits to advise on diet and lifestyle
e: MRI's negative predictive value depends on the underlying risk, so higher-risk men still need systematic biopsies.

o: The dorsal vein has three main branches: one superficial midline and two lateral
The prostate is covered by three fascial layers: Denonvilliers, prostatic and levator fascia
Denonvilliers fascia is densest at the base over the seminal vesicles, thinning towards the sphincter
Laterally the prostatic fascia stays separate from the levator fascia
e: Laterally the prostatic and levator fasciae fuse. Small pudendal branches met when opening the endopelvic fascia should be clipped, not cauterised, to protect the pudendal artery and nerve.

q: Which step is correct in open radical prostatectomy?
o: Pull the edges of the dorsal vein together in the midline
Never release the levator fascia high at the apex
Pull the prostate upward when releasing the neurovascular bundles

Roll the prostate side to side with a sponge stick and release the bundles with a right angle from the posterior surface, starting at the apex; divide the posterior branch over the seminal vesicles before the pedicles
e: Releasing the levator fascia high at the apex reduces traction and preserves the front nerve fibres, but may increase positive margins. Oversew the dorsal vein edges in a V.

q: Which statement about the anastomosis and lymph node dissection is correct?
o: If the anastomosis is under tension, put the catheter on traction

Relieve tension by freeing the bladder from the peritoneum; a Babcock clamp holding the bladder neck to the urethra while tying nearly eliminated bladder neck contracture; aim for mucosa-to-mucosa, watertight and tension-free
Lymph node dissection ends at the obturator nerve
Remove the lymphatics over the external iliac artery
e: The back limit of the node dissection is the hypogastric vein. Preserve the lymphatics over the external iliac artery, which drain the leg. Bladder neck contracture occurs in under 10%.

o: A randomised trial showed sural nerve grafts clearly improve potency
Accessory pudendal arteries should be preserved
In one series potency recovered from 42% at 3 months to 73% at 1 year
Post-prostatectomy PDE5 inhibitors on demand were preferred to daily use in the chapter
e: The trial found no difference. Grafts are placed in reversed orientation, and 26% of bilateral grafts gave erections adequate for penetration.

q: Which statement about radical perineal prostatectomy is FALSE?
o: Lower-limb sensory neurapraxia occurs in about 2% and is almost always transient
Patients should have scheduled rectal suppositories after surgery
Pulling on the Lowsley retractor while dividing the rectourethralis lifts the rectum and causes injury, so apply traction only after division
A rectal injury recognised and repaired in two layers allows the operation to continue
e: Avoid rectal stimulation after surgery. Most go home by day 2 on a quickly advanced diet. A red rubber catheter guides the anterior anastomotic sutures, and the Foley is passed only after they are tied.

o: Robotic prostatectomy gives worse potency than open surgery
Interfascial nerve sparing suits organ-confined disease; minimise thermal energy near the bundles
A running anastomosis needs only one knot
Higher cost comes mainly from longer operating time and disposables
e: The chapter reports statistically better potency with robotic surgery. Identify any median lobe before dividing the posterior bladder neck. Bladder neck reconstruction may be needed after TURP, a median lobe or a large gland. Urine leaks need longer catheterisation. A skilled bedside assistant is important.

o: Pollack's hypofractionation trial (70.2 Gy in 26 vs 76 Gy in 38) showed better PSA control with the short course
IMRT delivers less dose to the rectum, bladder and bowel than conformal radiotherapy
A PSA velocity over 2 ng/mL/year before treatment predicts failure
High-risk disease treated with radiotherapy alone had about 33% 5-year PSA failure-free survival (D'Amico 1998)
e: The shorter course did not improve 5-year biochemical failure, and caused more late urinary toxicity in men with poor baseline urinary function.

q: Thirty months after IMRT plus 6 months of ADT, a 58-year-old's PSA has risen 0.8 to 2.6 to 3.2 to 5.4 with recovered testosterone. Best step:
o: Benign bounce
Immediate salvage prostatectomy
Systemic staging (with prostate MRI), because the early, rapid rise suggests distant failure before any local salvage
Reassure: testosterone recovery
e: Bounces are typical after brachytherapy, not IMRT. A rectourethral fistula after combined EBRT and brachytherapy shows contrast passing from the prostatic urethra into the rectum on voiding cystourethrography.

o: Third-generation cryoprobes (17-gauge), adjustable ice length, real-time ice-edge monitoring and urethral warmers improved focal cryotherapy
PSA reliably confirms focal therapy success
Focal laser ablation gives predictable necrosis around the fibre tip; irreversible electroporation is non-thermal and spares connective tissue
TRUS biopsy is poor for planning focal therapy: it overdiagnoses, misses about 30% of significant cancers (anterior or apical) and repeats inconsistently
e: PSA is less useful after focal therapy. Focal therapy can be hemi-gland, quadrant or lesion-only. In-bore MRI-guided HIFU and TULSA are being studied. Brachytherapy, SBRT and nanoparticles are under investigation for focal use.

o: High-dose bicalutamide reduced progression in locally advanced disease
After prostatectomy with nodal disease, radiotherapy plus ADT may give the best survival
In the Kattan postoperative nomogram, a PSA of 17 contributes heavily to recurrence risk
Neoadjuvant ADT before prostatectomy improves biochemical survival
e: Neoadjuvant ADT reduces positive margins without improving biochemical survival, so it has no role before surgery. There is no evidence for adjuvant immunotherapy or chemotherapy after surgery.

o: LHRH analogues are made more potent by substituting the amino acid at position 6
Prophylactic breast radiotherapy treats established gynaecomastia
Once present, gynaecomastia may need simple mastectomy
ADT can cause bone loss, sexual dysfunction, hot flushes, cognitive decline, muscle loss, more body fat, anaemia, gynaecomastia, diabetes and cardiovascular deaths
e: Prophylactic radiotherapy (10 Gy) only prevents it. Combined androgen blockade is the most expensive form of ADT.

o: Progression-free survival is a better trial end point than response rate, and PSA is a poor marker of drug benefit
Androgen ablation causes apoptosis
The androgen receptor can be activated by oestrogens, progestins, growth factors and cytokines
Good functional status with normal haemoglobin and LDH predicts poor survival on docetaxel
e: Fit patients with no visceral disease and normal haemoglobin and LDH often live more than 2 years on docetaxel. After docetaxel, cabazitaxel can extend survival beyond 12 months.
